extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in comedy, race, and culture (KQED Arts & Culture audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and production-oriented principles for Black resistance humor — standup, sketch, TV and film work that uses comedy to critique racism and shift cultural power. Draws on historical precedent, character creation, risk-taking, and industry strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy as a form of Black resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy used as a form of Black resistance; a cultural expression dating back transgenerationally (19th century onward) that critiques white power structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article cites vaudeville-era comedians (Bert Williams, George Walker), playwright William Wells Brown, Frederick Douglass, and 20th-century figures (Moms Mabley, Redd Foxx, Dick Gregory, James Baldwin) as antecedents. Use humor to expose and challenge systemic injustices rather than merely entertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tackle the pressing social topic of race
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics should 'tackle the most pressing social topic: the issue of race in America.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paul Mooney advised Richard Pryor that addressing race was necessary to do 'something substantial' in comedy. Explicitly centering racial topics can be a deliberate creative choice to make work politically and culturally consequential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weave personal experience and pain into material
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting one's personal experience—specifically personal pain—in ways that 'make us think' while also provoking laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richard Pryor is highlighted for using his personal pain in routines to both provoke thought and elicit laughter; combining vulnerability and humor can deepen impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vernacular and contemporary slang to center culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite the rules of standup by weaving modern slang and Black cultural speech into routines to put Black culture front and center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stylistic choice helps authenticity and cultural resonance; credited to Richard Pryor's influence on later comedians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ satirical storytelling to combat oppression
rubrics_metrics.description: Use satire and satirical storytelling as a vehicle for social critique and resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Moms Mabley, Redd Foxx, Dick Gregory, and James Baldwin. Satire should be used to illuminate injustice and undermine power structures rather than simply mock marginalized people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create provocative characters that satirize societal archetypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop characters (e.g., Homey D. Clown) that subvert and satirize cultural archetypes to deliver social commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homey D. Clown is described as the 'anti–Ronald McDonald,' using acerbic jokes to shatter the veneer of childhood innocence and comment on anti-Black ideologies. Character-based satire can convey critique through exaggerated persona and catchphrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be outspoken and willing to offend as a deliberate strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Outspokenness and deliberate offense can be hallmarks of effective resistance humor ('equal opportunity offender'); upsetting some audiences may be evidence of doing challenging work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paul Mooney described his comedy as 'a nuclear bomb' and believed white audience walkouts signaled effectiveness. The article notes this can be double-edged: industry backlash and marginalization may follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept the risks of censorship and live-broadcast constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Pushing boundaries on live TV can provoke censorship measures (e.g., NBC's seven-second delay after Pryor/Mooney material).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using profanity or controversial content on live platforms may trigger institutional responses; creators should weigh impact versus potential suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage industry connections and celebrity to shift representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use star power and Hollywood connections to center African Americans in mainstream films and media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eddie Murphy is credited with leveraging connections to place Black stories at the center of blockbusters (e.g., Boomerang, Coming to America). Strategic career moves and industry influence can broaden cultural impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate and form collectives to amplify impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Working as an ensemble or collective (e.g., 'The Black Pack') can shift popular culture and the entertainment industry more effectively than isolated acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes how the group of five comedians' combined body of work altered Hollywood and influenced later generations; complementary talents (writing, performing, producing) in a group can produce systemic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate diverse strengths: creativity, charisma, ingenuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinct personal strengths—creativity, charisma, ingenuity—contribute to a collective or individual comedian's success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keenen Ivory Wayans' creativity, Arsenio Hall's charisma, and Robert Townsend's ingenuity are highlighted; different skill sets (performing, writing, producing) play roles in cultural influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentorship and behind-the-scenes influence matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Influential mentorship and behind-the-scenes writing shaping a comic's voice are critical (e.g., Paul Mooney's role mentoring Pryor and writing for others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mooney's contributions—naming the group, shaping characters, writing for shows—underscore the importance of less-visible creative labor in producing pioneering resistance comedy.
